title: Needing Someone Does Not Mean Owning Them
deck: Need can give rise to requests and responsibilities, but cannot turn another person’s future into a right of your own.
body: Need can deepen a relationship.

Someone may be your most important companion, the first person you think of when facing difficulties, and a condition that enables many arrangements in your life to continue. Acknowledging this need is not weakness. People do not live entirely independently in the first place.
But need can also easily be misrepresented as a right.
“I cannot manage without you, so you cannot leave.”
“You know I need you. Why would you still make this choice?”
At this point, one person’s vulnerability begins to lay claim to another person’s future.
The need is real, but being real does not automatically give you possession of the other person.

You can explain what you depend on and ask for support. If both people have already made commitments, dependence may also give rise to specific responsibilities. You cannot first let someone build their life around a promise and then suddenly pretend you have nothing to do with each other.
But responsibility and ownership remain different.

Responsibility requires you to face honestly what your actions will cause, provide the necessary explanations, and take responsibility for consequences you have already brought about together. Ownership, by contrast, says: as long as my life cannot do without you, you no longer have the right to change direction.
The former acknowledges that two lives have become connected. The latter understands that connection to mean that one person belongs to the other.
We cross this boundary so easily because need brings fear.

When someone important might leave, what we stand to lose is not only the relationship. It may also be the stability of our lives, our imagined future, or even the way we understand ourselves. To prevent this loss, we turn our pain into the other person’s obligation.
“If you leave, I will be hurt” is true.
“So you have no right to leave,” however, still requires a further reason.
Feelings can show how far-reaching the consequences of a choice will be. They cannot, on their own, determine what another person must choose.
This does not mean that leaving is always solely the departing person’s business.

Shared caregiving, shared resources, explicit promises, and long-term dependence all create responsibilities that must be borne when leaving. You can end a relationship, but the freedom to end it does not entitle you to leave the transition, explanations, and consequences already caused entirely to the person who stays.
Freedom does not mean suddenly treating a shared life as though it had never been shared.
But even a heavy responsibility cannot be extended indefinitely into “You must stay forever.”

Some people ultimately continue a relationship out of responsibility alone. They no longer want to, but believe that leaving would make the other person unable to manage their life. Staying appears to prove love, while in fact both people are trapped in need.
The person who needs the other becomes increasingly afraid of independence, while the one who stays feels increasingly possessed.
Such a relationship may still contain care, but genuine choice becomes difficult.
Loving someone therefore sometimes also involves taking your own needs seriously.

Do I need their companionship, or do I need them never to be able to refuse me? Do I hope they will stay, or demand that by staying they guarantee I will never face uncertainty? Which dependencies arise from our shared commitments, and which have become things I am unwilling to bear on my own?
These questions will not make the need disappear.
They simply put it back in the position of a request rather than a command.
“I need you very much, and I hope you will stay.”
This sentence can carry great weight while still leaving the other person room to answer.
“Because I need you, you belong to me.”
This sentence turns one person’s vulnerability into a boundary around the other.
A good relationship does not require people to have no need for each other at all.

Having no need at all is not necessarily freedom either. Sometimes it is simply a refusal to let anyone truly enter your life. People can depend deeply on one another, make each other important conditions of their lives, and take on responsibilities that go beyond personal convenience because of their commitments.
But dependence must still recognize two people who cannot replace each other.
I can entrust much of my life to you, but that does not allow me to turn you into my resource. You can promise companionship and still remain someone who changes, grows tired, and reconsiders.
Needing someone means acknowledging the weight they carry in your life.
Owning someone means denying that they still have a life you do not determine.
The two may seem only one step apart. Whether a relationship still has room for two people often depends on whether that step has been taken.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
